la:adv:palam.gloss: without concealment, openly, publicly, undisguisedly, plainly, unambiguously
senses: without concealment, openly, publicly, undisguisedly, plainly, unambiguously
la:adv:palam.html:
pălam, adv. and prep.
locative form; cf.: clam, perperam, etc.; root pal-, pla-; as in πλατύς, planus; cf. pellis; hence, on the surface, on the open plain, and so
,
openly, publicly, undisguisedly, plainly (cf.: publice, vulgo, aperte; opp.: clam, occulte, secreto, etc.; class.).
Lit.: haec quae in foro palam Syracusis ... gesta sunt,: auferre argentum palam atque aperte,; so, non ex insidiis, sed aperte ac palam elaboratur,; and: palam agere coepit et aperte dicere occidendum Milonem,; cf. also : PALAM LVCI, Tab. Bant. vers. 15; so ib. vers. 22; cf.: arma in templum Castoris luce palam comportarentur,: ut luce palam in foro saltet,: gaudia clamque palamque, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 247 Vahl.); : non per praestigias, sed palam,: non occulte sed palam,, § 49: palam ... obscurius,: bestiae furtim fruuntur (frumento), domini palam et libere,: palam ante oculos omnium,; : nec palam nec secreto,; cf. : palam ... intus,: quod palam abnuerat inter secreta convivii largitur,, in late Lat.: in palam,; . —
Transf.
Palam est or factum est, it is public, well known: palam est res,: haec commemoro quae sunt palam,: palam ante oculos omnium esse,: palam factum est,: hāc re palam factā,; cf.: palam facere suis, quo loco Eumenes esset,: hujus de morte ut palam factum est,; cf.: cum exspirasset Tarquinius, celatā morte, suas opes firmavit: tum demum palam factum est, etc.,: et nondum palam facto vivi mortuique,: cui palam facti parricidii obnoxius erat,; so (euphemist.), ut de Claudio palam factum est, when the death of Claudius was announced: cogitur Cato incumbens gladio simul de se ac de republicā palam facere,: idem nobis prophetae palam faciunt,.—With subject-clause: pisces audire palam est,it is well known,: dicere,to say openly,: palam ferente Hannibale ab se Minucium, se ab Fabio victum,making no secret of it,.—
Prep., with abl., analogous to clam and coram, before, in the presence of one (not ante-Aug., and mostly poet.): te palam,: meque palam de me tuto male saepe loquuntur,: meque palam,: Marte palam,; : rem creditori palam populo solvit,: palam omnibus,: palam senatu,.

la:noun:palus.gloss: swamp, marsh, morass, bog, fen, pool
senses: swamp, marsh, morass, bog, fen, pool
la:noun:palus.html:
pālus, i, m. (
neutr. collat. form pālum, i, Varr. ap. ) [for paglus (cf. dim. paxillus); root pag-; Sanscr. pācas, snare; Gr. πήγνυμι, fasten; Lat. pango; cf.: pignus, pax], a stake, prop, stay, pale.
Lit. (very freq. and class.; syn.: sudes, stipes): ut figam palum in parietem,; : damnati ad supplicium traditi, ad palum alligati,: palis adjungere vitem, (7), 33; : palos et ridicas dolare,; . 1.—The Roman soldiers learned to fight by attacking a stake set in the ground, ; ; hence, aut quis non vidit vulnera pali?.—And, transf.: exerceamur ad palum: et, ne imparatos fortuna deprehendat, fiat nobis paupertas familiaris, .—In the lang. of gladiators, palus primus or palusprimus (called also machaera Herculeana, ), a gladiator's sword of wood, borne by the secutores, whence their leader was also called primus palus, ; Inscr. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 694.—Prov.: quasi palo pectus tundor, of one astonished, stunned,.—
Transf., = membrum virile, .

senses: to caress, flatter, coax, wheedle; soothe
la:verb:palpo.html:
palpo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., and pal-por, ātus
palpus; cf. Gr. ψάλλω
, 1,
v. dep. a., to stroke, to touch softly, to pat (poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn. mulceo).
Lit.: modo pectora praebet Virgineā palpanda manu, Jahn N. cr.: palpate lupos,: cum equum permulsit quis vel palpatus est,: tamquam si manu palpetur, Schol. : animalia blandi manu palpata magistri, Prud. στεφ. 11, 91.—
Transf.
To caress, coax, wheedle, flatter.
Absol.: hoc sis vide ut palpatur! nullus est quando occepit, blandior,; Lucil. ap. : palpabo, ecquonam modo possim, etc.,: nihil asperum tetrumque palpanti est,.—
With dat.: quam blande mulieri palpabitur,: cui male si palpere, recalcitrat undique tutus,: scribenti palpare, Poll. ap. .—
With acc.: quem munere palpat Carus,; .—
To feel one's way (late Lat.): et palpes in meridie, sicut palpare solet caecus in tenebris,; id. Job, 5, 14.
la:verb:palpo.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., ātus, v. dep. a.

la:noun:palla.gloss: A rectangular piece of cloth worn by ladies in Ancient Rome and fastened with brooches.
senses: A rectangular piece of cloth worn by ladies in Ancient Rome and fastened with brooches.
la:noun:palla.html:
palla, ae, f.
kindred with pellis; cf. Doed. Syn. 5, p. 211
,
a long and wide upper garment of the Roman ladies, held together by brooches, a robe, mantle (cf.: stola, peplum, chlamys),; ; ; ; ; : pro longae tegmine pallae Tigridis exuviae per dorsum a vertice pendent,: palla superba,: obscura,: scissā pallā,; cf. Becker, Gall. 3, p. 144 (2d edit.).—
Transf.
In the poets also of a garment worn by men, e. g. of the dress of a tragic actor: personae pallaeque repertor honestae Aeschylus,; ; ; of the cithara-player Arion, ; of Phœbus, ; ; ; of Boreas, ; of Mercury, ; of Osiris, ; of Bacchus, ; of Jason, .—
An under-garment: citharoedus palla inaurata indutus,: pallamque induta rigentem insuper aurato circumvelatur amictu,; : Gallica,; ; .—
A curtain: περιπέτασμα, velum, palla, Gloss. Philox.: cum inter dicentes et audientem palla interesset,.

senses: a linear measure, palm, of various exact values throughout Europe but usually one quarter of the local foot.
la:noun:palma.html:
palma, ae
παλάμη; Sanscr. phal, to open
, f.,
the palm of the hand.
Lit., ; : cavis undam de flumine palmis Sustulit,: aliquem palmā concutere,: faciem contundere palmā,: os hominis liberi manus suae palmā verberare, Laber. ap. . —
Transf.
(Pars pro toto.) The hand: compressan' palma an porrecta ferio?: palmarum intentus,: passis palmis salutem petere,: teneras arcebant vincula palmas,: duplices tendens ad sidera palmas,: amplexus tremulis altaria palmis,; .—
The sole of a goose's foot: palmas pedum anseris torrere,.—
The broad end or blade of an oar: palmarum pulsus, Laber. ap. : caerula verrentes abiegnis aequora palmis,; .—
A palm-tree, a palm, φοῖνιξ: ab ejus summo, sicut palmae, rami quam late diffunduntur,; : in palmarum foliis primo scriptitatum,; ; : arbor palmae,: ardua,: viridis,: arbusto palmarum dives Idume,.—Sing. collect.: umbrosa,.—Hence,
Transf.
The fruit of the palm-tree, a date (poet.): quid vult palma sibi rugosaque carica,; .—
A palm-branch, e. g. which was suspended in wine to make it sweeter, ; .—
Hence, also, a broom made of palm-twigs: ten' lapides varios lutulentā radere palmā, (pro scopis ex palmā confectis, Schol.); .—
A palm-branch or palm-wreath, as a token of victory: eodem anno (461 A.U.C.) ... palmae primum, translato e Graeciā more, victoribus datae,; cf.: more victorum cum palmā discucurrit,: IMP. CAES. EX SICILIA EID. NOV. TRIVMPHAVIT, PALMAM DEDIT, dedicated to Jupiter, Inscr. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 607; so very frequently: palmam dare, Tabulae Fastorum Triumph., v. Bullet. Instit. Archaeol. 1861, p. 91; cf. ; hence,
Transf., a token or badge of victory, the palm or prize; and still more gen., victory, honor, glory, pre-eminence: antehac est habitus parcus ... is nunc in aliam partem palmam possidet,: plurimarum palmarum gladiator,: cum palmam jam primus acceperit,: quos Elea domum reducit Palma caelestes,: quam palmam utinam di immortales tibi reservent,: docto oratori palma danda est,; ; : alicujus rei palmam alicui deferre,; cf. : palmā donare aliquem,: arbiter pugnae posuisse nudo Sub pede palmam Fertur,. —Of things: Siculum mel fert palmam,bears away the palm, has the preference,.—
Hence, in gen., the topmost twig or branch of any tree: quae cujusque stipitis palma sit,; cf. (Mütz.)—
Poet., of the victor himself: post Helymus subit et jam tertia palma Diores,; .—
Of horses: Eliadum palmae equarum,.—
Also, of one about to be conquered, and who is to become the prize of the victor: ultima restabat fusis jam palma duobus Virbius,.—
A branch on a tree, esp. on a vine, = palmes, ; ; ; ; sq.—
The fruit of an Egyptian tree, .—
An aromatic plant growing in Africa and Syria, (= elate).—
A marine plant, .—
A town in the Balearic islands, .

palmo, no
perf., ātum, 1, v. a.

.

To tie up a vine: palmare hoc est materias alligare,.—Hence, palmātus, a, um, P. a.
Marked with the palm of a hand: palmatus paries, bearing the mark of a (bloody) hand, and 12, pp. 30 and 31 Burm.: cervi palmati,with antlers shaped like the palm of a hand,—
Containing the figure of a palm-tree: lapis,.—
Worked or embroidered with palmbranches: tunica, usually worn by generals in their triumphal processions,; fin.: togae,: vestis,, n. 5.—Also, subst.: palmāta, ae, f., ; ; ; ; : palmatus consul, clothed with the palmata tunica, : statua, Treb. Poll. .

la:adj:pallidus.html:
pallĭdus, a, um, adj.
palleo
,
pale, pallid (cf.: lividus, luridus).
Lit.: vides ut pallidus omnis Cenā desurgat dubiā,: ora buxo Pallidiora,; : Asturii scrutator pallidus auri,; : recto vultu et pallidus, i. e. well or sick, : oriens,: stellae, quae sunt omnium pallidissimae,.—Esp. of the Lower World: pallida turba,: ditis profundi Pallida regna,: pallida Leti loca, Enn. ap. Müll. (Trag. Rel. v. 109 Vahl.): equus,.—
Transf.
That makes pale, pallid: pallida mors,: vina,: aconita,.—
Musty, mouldy: vetustate ficus fit pallidior,.—
Livid: hospes inauratā pallidior statuā,. —
Trop.
Pale with love, in love, : pallidus in lentā Naïde Daphnis erat,; . —
Pale with fright, affrighted, ; .

la:noun:Pallas.html:
Pallăs, ădis and ădos, f., = Παλλάς.
Surname of the Greek goddess Athene, and hence of the corresponding Minerva of the Romans, the goddess of war and wisdom; the inventress of working in wool, and of the cultivation of the olive, on which account the olive-tree was sacred to her: Pallas Minerva est dicta, quod Pallantem Gigantem interfecerit, vel, sicut putabant, quod in Pallante palude nata est, Müll.: Pallas . . . Proeliis audax,; : Palladis ales,the owl,: Pallados arbor,the olive-tree,; cf.: rami Palladis,: iratā Pallade, i. q. invitā Minervā,.—
Transf.
Oil: infusā Pallade,: pinguis,.—
The olive-tree: dat quoque baciferam Pallada rarus ager,.—
The Palladium: Helenum raptā cum Pallade captum,: Pallade conspectā,.—
The number seven, ; .—
For Vesta, because the Palladium stood in the temple of Vesta: Pallados ignes, Prop 4 (5), 4, 45.—
Deriv.
Pallădĭus, a, um, adj., = Παλλάδιος, of or belonging to Pallas, Palladian: numen Palladium,i. e. Pallas,: aegis,of Pallas,: Palladiā gaudent silvā vivacis olivae,; latices,oil,: corona,an olive-wreath,: arx,Troy, (4, 8), 42: arces,Athens,: honores,shown to Pallas,: pinus, the Argo, because built under Minerva's direction, : metus,inspired by Pallas,: forum, the Roman forum, because there stood a temple of Minerva, : Palladia Alba, because Domitian caused the Quinquatria in honor of Pallas to be annually celebrated there,; cf. : Palladia Tolosa, because the sciences flourished there,: manus,i. e. skilful,: ars,: lotos,the flute,.—
Subst.: Pallădĭum, ii, n., the image or statue of Pallas, which, in the reign of Ilus, fell from heaven at Troy, and during the Trojan war was carried off by Ulysses and Diomed, because the fate of the city depended on the possession of this image. It afterwards came from Greece to Rome, where Metellus saved it from the temple of Vesta when the latter was burned down, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. ; .

la:noun:palaestra.gloss: wrestling school, palaestra; place of exercise; gymnasium
senses: wrestling school, palaestra; place of exercise; gymnasium
rhetorical exercises; school of rhetoric, school
la:noun:palaestra.html:
pălaestra, ae, f., = παλαίστρα,
a wrestling-school, wrestling-place, place of exercise, palœstra, where youths, with their bodies naked and anointed with oil, practised gymnastic exercises. Such palæstrae were also attached to private houses: in palaestram venire,; cf. : in palaestrā atque in foro,: statuas in palaestrā ponere,: pars in gramineis exercent membra palaestris,. —Of the palæstrae in private houses, : (Fibrenus) tantum complectitur quod satis sit modicae palaestrae loci,; .—
Transf.
A wrestling in the palæstra, the exercise of wrestling: non utuntur in ipsā lusione artificio proprio palaestrae, sed indicat ipse motus, didicerintne palaestram an nesciant,: exercent patrias oleo labente palaestras Nudati socii,: corpora agresti nudant palaestrae,: uncta palaestra,: nitidā palaestrā ludere,; cf. .—Mercury was regarded as the founder of wrestling combats, ; .—
In the lang. of comedy, a brothel, ; .—
Exercises in the school of rhetoric, rhetorical exercises, a school of rhetoric, a school: nitidum genus verborum sed palaestrae magis et olei, quam hujus civilis turbae ac fori,: non tam armis institutus, quam palaestrā,: sic adjuvet, ut palaestra histrionem,; ; cf. : Antipater habuit (in scribendā historiā) vires agrestes ille quidem atque horridas sine nitore ac palaestrā,

.—*

An art or skill: utemur eā palaestrā, quam a te didicimus,.

pallor, ōris, m.

Pallor, personified as the god of fear, ; .

la:other:Palma.html:
palma, ae
παλάμη; Sanscr. phal, to open
, f.,
the palm of the hand.
Lit., ; : cavis undam de flumine palmis Sustulit,: aliquem palmā concutere,: faciem contundere palmā,: os hominis liberi manus suae palmā verberare, Laber. ap. . —
Transf.
(Pars pro toto.) The hand: compressan' palma an porrecta ferio?: palmarum intentus,: passis palmis salutem petere,: teneras arcebant vincula palmas,: duplices tendens ad sidera palmas,: amplexus tremulis altaria palmis,; .—
The sole of a goose's foot: palmas pedum anseris torrere,.—
The broad end or blade of an oar: palmarum pulsus, Laber. ap. : caerula verrentes abiegnis aequora palmis,; .—
A palm-tree, a palm, φοῖνιξ: ab ejus summo, sicut palmae, rami quam late diffunduntur,; : in palmarum foliis primo scriptitatum,; ; : arbor palmae,: ardua,: viridis,: arbusto palmarum dives Idume,.—Sing. collect.: umbrosa,.—Hence,
Transf.
The fruit of the palm-tree, a date (poet.): quid vult palma sibi rugosaque carica,; .—
A palm-branch, e. g. which was suspended in wine to make it sweeter, ; .—
Hence, also, a broom made of palm-twigs: ten' lapides varios lutulentā radere palmā, (pro scopis ex palmā confectis, Schol.); .—
A palm-branch or palm-wreath, as a token of victory: eodem anno (461 A.U.C.) ... palmae primum, translato e Graeciā more, victoribus datae,; cf.: more victorum cum palmā discucurrit,: IMP. CAES. EX SICILIA EID. NOV. TRIVMPHAVIT, PALMAM DEDIT, dedicated to Jupiter, Inscr. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 607; so very frequently: palmam dare, Tabulae Fastorum Triumph., v. Bullet. Instit. Archaeol. 1861, p. 91; cf. ; hence,
Transf., a token or badge of victory, the palm or prize; and still more gen., victory, honor, glory, pre-eminence: antehac est habitus parcus ... is nunc in aliam partem palmam possidet,: plurimarum palmarum gladiator,: cum palmam jam primus acceperit,: quos Elea domum reducit Palma caelestes,: quam palmam utinam di immortales tibi reservent,: docto oratori palma danda est,; ; : alicujus rei palmam alicui deferre,; cf. : palmā donare aliquem,: arbiter pugnae posuisse nudo Sub pede palmam Fertur,. —Of things: Siculum mel fert palmam,bears away the palm, has the preference,.—
Hence, in gen., the topmost twig or branch of any tree: quae cujusque stipitis palma sit,; cf. (Mütz.)—
Poet., of the victor himself: post Helymus subit et jam tertia palma Diores,; .—
Of horses: Eliadum palmae equarum,.—
Also, of one about to be conquered, and who is to become the prize of the victor: ultima restabat fusis jam palma duobus Virbius,.—
A branch on a tree, esp. on a vine, = palmes, ; ; ; ; sq.—
The fruit of an Egyptian tree, .—
An aromatic plant growing in Africa and Syria, (= elate).—
A marine plant, .—
A town in the Balearic islands, .

la:other:Palaemon.gloss: Palaemon, a sea god who was the son of Athamus and Ino
senses: Palaemon, a sea god who was the son of Athamus and Ino
la:other:Palaemon.html:
Pălaemon, ŏnis, m., = Παλαίμων.
A sea-god, formerly called Melicerta, the son of Athamas and Ino: O Palaemon, sancte Neptuni comes,; ; ; ; .—Hence,
Pălae-mŏnĭus, a, um, of or belonging to the seagod Palœmon, poet. for Corinthian, : Palaemoniae coronae,won at the Isthmian games, which were celebrated in honor of Palœmon,.—
Remmius Palaemon, a Roman grammarian in the time of Tiberius and Claudius, ; ; ; ; ; .—
A shepherd, .

la:noun:Palinurus.html:
Pălĭnūrus, i, m., = Παλίνουρος,
the pilot of Æneas, who fell asleep at the helm and tumbled into the sea off the coast of Lucania, whence the name of the promontory near the spot (now perh. Punta dello Spartimento), ; ; ; 381; ; ; . —In a lusus verbb. with πάλιν οὐρεῖν, iterum meiere, .

la:noun:palus#2.html:
pālus, i, m. (
neutr. collat. form pālum, i, Varr. ap. ) [for paglus (cf. dim. paxillus); root pag-; Sanscr. pācas, snare; Gr. πήγνυμι, fasten; Lat. pango; cf.: pignus, pax], a stake, prop, stay, pale.
Lit. (very freq. and class.; syn.: sudes, stipes): ut figam palum in parietem,; : damnati ad supplicium traditi, ad palum alligati,: palis adjungere vitem, (7), 33; : palos et ridicas dolare,; . 1.—The Roman soldiers learned to fight by attacking a stake set in the ground, ; ; hence, aut quis non vidit vulnera pali?.—And, transf.: exerceamur ad palum: et, ne imparatos fortuna deprehendat, fiat nobis paupertas familiaris, .—In the lang. of gladiators, palus primus or palusprimus (called also machaera Herculeana, ), a gladiator's sword of wood, borne by the secutores, whence their leader was also called primus palus, ; Inscr. Marin. Fratr. Arv. p. 694.—Prov.: quasi palo pectus tundor, of one astonished, stunned,.—
Transf., = membrum virile, .

la:verb:palleo.gloss: to be pale; to turn pale, blanch
senses: to be pale; to turn pale, blanch
to grow pale, be anxious, be fearful
to fade, lose color, change color
la:verb:palleo.html:
pallĕo, ui, 2, v. n.
Sanscr. palitas, gray; Gr. πελλός, πελιδνός, πολιός; cf. pullus
,
to be or look pale.
Lit.: sudat, pallet,: pallent amisso sanguine venae,: metu sceleris futuri,: timore,: mea rugosa pallebunt ora senectā,; morbo,: fame,.— Esp. of lovers: palleat omnis amans; hic est color aptus amanti,must look pale,; .—Also through indolence, .—
Transf.
To be or look sallow, or yellow: saxum quoque palluit auro,: arca palleat nummis,; ; so, to become turbid: Tagus auriferis pallet turbatus arenis,.—
To lose its natural color, to change color, to fade: et numquam Herculeo numine pallet ebur,always remains white,sidera pallent,: ne vitio caeli palleat aegra seges,: pallet nostris Aurora venenis,: pallere diem, Luc 7, 177—
With acc.: multos pallere colores,to change color often,.—
Trop.
To grow pale, be sick with desire, to long for, eagerly desire any thing: ambitione malā aut argenti pallet amore,: nummo,.—
To grow pale at any thing, to be anxious or fearful.—With dat.: pueris,i. e. on account of,: ad omnia fulgura,: Marco sub judice palles?.—
With acc.: scatentem Belluis pontum,: fraternos ictus,; .—
To grow pale by excessive application to a thing: iratum Eupoliden praegrandi cum sene palles,read yourself pale over Eupolis,: nunc utile multis Pallere, i. e. studere,: vigilandum, nitendum, pallendum est,of close study,.—Hence, pallens, entis, P. a., pale, wan (poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Lit.: simulacra modis pallentia miris,: umbrae Erebi,: animae,: regna,of the Lower World,; cf. undae,i. e. the Styx, the Cocytus,: persona,: pallens morte futurā,: pallentes terrore puellae,. —
Transf.
Of a faint or pale color, pale-colored, greenish, yellowish, darkcolored: pallentes violae,: arva,: gemmā e viridi pallens,: hedera,: herbae,: lupini,: faba,: sol jungere pallentes equos,: toga,.—
Poet., that makes pale: morbi,: philtra,: curae,: oscula,.—
Trop., pale, weak, bad: fama,pale,: mores,bad, vicious,.

la:noun:palmes.html:
palmĕs, ĭtis, m.
1. palma, II. E.
,
a young branch or shoot of a vine, a vinesprig, vine-sprout (syn. pampinus).
Lit.: palmites vitium sarmenta appellantur, quod in modum palmarum humanarum virgulas quasi digitos edunt, Müll.: palmitum duo genera sunt, alterum pampinarium, alterum fructuarium,; ; ; ; : jam laeto turgent in palmite gemmae,: stratus humi palmes, Juv.

8, 78; : ego sum vitis, vos palmites,.—

Transf.
A vine; a vineyard: Icario nemorosus palmite Gaurus,; .—
In gen., a bough, branch: crudus arboris,: palmites arborum, (where Mützell reads palmas); : opaco palmite bacae,.

la:noun:palatum.html:
pălātum, i, n., and (rarely) pălātus, i, m.
perh. from root pa-of pasco
,
the palate.
Lit.: suave domini,: nec enim sequitur, ut, cui cor sapiat, ei non sapiat palatus,: quae (voluptas) palato percipiatur,: boum dare membra palato,: subtile palatum,: nigra subest udo tantum cui lingua palato,; ; cf.: cum balba feris annoso verba palato,: torpente palato,.—In plur.: palata docta et erudita,.—
Trop., the palate, as the organ of taste and judgment: (Epicurus) dum palato quid sit optimum judicat,: orationis condimentum, quod sentitur latente judicio velut palato,.—*
Transf. (of the form of the palate), a vault: caeli, Enn. ap. (, n. 19 Vahl.).

pālo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
1. palus

la:verb:palor.gloss: to wander up and down or about, straggle, stray
senses: to wander up and down or about, straggle, stray
la:verb:palor.html:
pālor, ātus (
gen. plur. part. palantūm, ), 1, v. dep. (act. collat. form pālo, āre, Wernsd.; Poët. Lat. Min. 3, p. 90) [cf. Sanscr. pad, go; Gr. ποῦς, ποδός; Lat. pes], to wander up and down, to wander, wander about; to be dispersed, to straggle (not in Cic. or Cæs.; most freq. in part. pres.; syn.: vagor, erro).
Lit.: palantes comites quom montes inter opacos Quaerimus et magna dispersos voce ciemus,; cf. : vagi per agros palantur,; cf.: vagi palantesque per agros,; ; : agmen per agros palatur,: palantes in agris oppressit,: palantes extra castra,: boves palati ab suis gregibus,: palatos aggressus,: ex fugā palati,; : palantes error de tramite pellit,: terga dabant palantia Teucri,: palantia sidera,; so, palantesque polo stellas,; : palanti amni (Nilo),: insectari palantes hostes,: palantia monstra,.—
Trop.: errare atque viam palantes quaerere vitae,: palantes homines passim ac rationis egentes,.

la:noun:palatium.html:
Pălātĭum (Pāl- or Pall-, ; ), ĭi, n., = Παλάτιον, Παλλάντιον [root pa-, to protect, nourish; Sanscr. pala, shepherd; cf. Gr. αἰ-πόλος οἰο-πόλος;
Lat. pasco],one of the seven hills of Rome, that which was first built upon, Müll.; cf.: Palatium id est mons Romae, appellatus est, quod ibi pecus pascens balare consueverit, vel quod palare, id est errare, ibi pecudes solerent; alii, quod ibi Hyperborei filia Palanto habitaverit, quae ex Hercule Latinum peperit, alii eundem, quod Pallas ibi sepultus sit, aestimant appellari, Müll.—Augustus had his residence on the Palatine; hence, since the Aug. period,
Transf.: pălātĭum, ii, n., a palace: palatia fulgent,: secreta palatia matris,the temple of Cybele,: magni palatia caeli, the palace of the sky (of the seat of Jupiter), ; et saep.—
Deriv. Pălātīnus (Pāl- or Pall-, ; ; ; 9, 86, 7; 11, 8, 5; 13, 91, 1), a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Palatium, Palatine: pastores, Müll.: Evander,: colles,: aves,the vultures which Remus saw on the Palatium,: Apollo, so called because he had a temple on the Palatine Hill, built by Augustus, in which also was a library founded by him,; : dei,: ludi,which Livia caused to be celebrated in honor of Augustus,: colossus,the colossal statue of Nero, on the Palatium,; cf. ; : Palatina pars urbis, the tenth region, also called simply Palatina, : Palatina tribus, one of the four city tribes: Calvu' Palatina vir nobilis ac bonu' bello, Lucil. ap. : C. Claudius C. F. Palatina,; et saep.—Subst.: Pălātīni,ōrum, m., the people of the Palatine Mount, .—
Transf., of or belonging to the imperial palace, imperial: palatina laurus,which stood in front of the imperial palace,: atriensis,: domus,: cubile,: officia,offices about the court,; Treb. Gall. 17.—As subst.: Pălātīnus, i, m., an officer of the palace, a chamberlain: Parthenius palatinus, Domitian's chamberlain, ; cf. : Tonans,i. e. Domitian,.

la:verb:pallesco.html:
pallesco, pallăi, 3,
v. inch. n. [palleo], to grow or turn pale.
Lit.: ut qui timent

sanguine ex ore decedente pallescant, : pallescere curis,: nullā pallescere culpā,: pallescet super his,will turn pale with emotion,: umbraticā vitā pallescere,; .—

Transf., to turn pale, sallow: pallescunt frondes,wither, fade,: viso pallescit flamma veneno,; .

la:adj:palliatus.html:
pallĭātus, a, um, adj.
id.
,
dressed in a pallium, cloaked, usually said of Greeks.
Lit.: isti Graeci palliati,: Graeculus judex modo palliatus, modo togatus,; : Pythagoras,: palliata signa Phidiae,: illi palliati topiariam facere videantur,i. e. Grecian statues,: fabulae palliatae, comedies in which Greek characters were introduced in the Greek dress (opp. the fabulae togatae, in which Roman manners and dresses predominated), Varr. ap. P.; Don. Fragm. ante Comm. in Ter.—
Trop., covered, protected, .

la:noun:pallium.html:
pallium, i, n.,
a covering, cover [cf. palla].
In gen.
A coverlet: et gravius justo pallia pondus habent,: onerosa pallia jactat,: tunc queror in toto non sidere pallia lecto,; .—
A pall: arrepto pallio retexi corpora,; .—
A curtain: quae festis suspendam pallia portis?.—
In partic., a Greek cloak or mantle, esp. as the dress of the Grecian philosophers. The Romans were accustomed to wear it only when they resided among Greeks. It was also the dress of the hetaerae, both Greek and Roman, ; ; : pallium in collum conicere (as was customary with persons about to exert themselves),: soleas mihi late: pallium inice in me huc,; : umerum pallio onerare, : cum iste cum pallio purpureo talarique tunicā versaretur in conviviis muliebribus,: consularis homo soccos habuit et pallium,: amica corpus ejus texit suo pallio,: cum pallio et crepidis inambulare in gymnasio,: togam veteres ad calceos usque demittebant ut Graeci pallium,.—Fig.: solos esse Atticos credunt quādam eloquentiae frugalitate contentos, ac semper manum intra pallium continentis,speaking with calmness and reserve,; cf. .—Plur. for sing., .—Prov.: tunica propior pallio est,the shirt is nearer than the coat,: a togā ad pallium,of sinking from a high to a lower rank,.—
Transf.
The toga, and, in gen., an upper garment of any kind, ; ; ; 11, 23, 12.—
Since the pallium was the philosopher's cloak, a philosophic career or habit: ad pallium reverti,.

la:noun:pale.html:
pălē, ēs, f., = πάλη,
a wrestling (in post-Aug. poets): unctā pale,: liquidam nodare (al. nudare) palen,: jocos, palem, rudentem,.

la:verb:palpito.gloss: to move frequently and quickly, tremble, throb, pulsate, palpitate
senses: to move frequently and quickly, tremble, throb, pulsate, palpitate
la:verb:palpito.html:
palpĭto, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. freq. n. [palpo], to move frequently and quickly, to tremble, throb, pant, palpitate.
Lit.: cor palpitat, * : radix micat ultima linguae, Utque salire solet mutilatae cauda colubrae, Palpitat,: cerebrum uni homini in infantiā palpitat,: in ovo gutta sanguinis salit palpitatque,; .—Esp. of persons or animals in the agony of death, to struggle, be convulsed: palpitat et positas aspergit sanguine mensas,: semianimes palpitantesque,: jam palpitat arvis Phaedimus,; ; .—In mal. part., .—Of things: hic arduus ignis Palpitat,flickers,.—
Trop.: animum palpitantem percussit,.

la:other:Palaestra.gloss: a female given name, character in the play Rudens of Plautus
senses: a female given name, character in the play Rudens of Plautus
la:other:Palaestra.html:
pălaestra, ae, f., = παλαίστρα,
a wrestling-school, wrestling-place, place of exercise, palœstra, where youths, with their bodies naked and anointed with oil, practised gymnastic exercises. Such palæstrae were also attached to private houses: in palaestram venire,; cf. : in palaestrā atque in foro,: statuas in palaestrā ponere,: pars in gramineis exercent membra palaestris,. —Of the palæstrae in private houses, : (Fibrenus) tantum complectitur quod satis sit modicae palaestrae loci,; .—
Transf.
A wrestling in the palæstra, the exercise of wrestling: non utuntur in ipsā lusione artificio proprio palaestrae, sed indicat ipse motus, didicerintne palaestram an nesciant,: exercent patrias oleo labente palaestras Nudati socii,: corpora agresti nudant palaestrae,: uncta palaestra,: nitidā palaestrā ludere,; cf. .—Mercury was regarded as the founder of wrestling combats, ; .—
In the lang. of comedy, a brothel, ; .—
Exercises in the school of rhetoric, rhetorical exercises, a school of rhetoric, a school: nitidum genus verborum sed palaestrae magis et olei, quam hujus civilis turbae ac fori,: non tam armis institutus, quam palaestrā,: sic adjuvet, ut palaestra histrionem,; ; cf. : Antipater habuit (in scribendā historiā) vires agrestes ille quidem atque horridas sine nitore ac palaestrā,

.—*

An art or skill: utemur eā palaestrā, quam a te didicimus,.

la:adj:palaestricus.gloss: Of or pertaining to the palaestra.
senses: Of or pertaining to the palaestra.
la:adj:palaestricus.html:
pălaestrĭcus, a, um, adj., = παλαιστρικος,
of or belonging to the palœstra, palœstric: pro exercitu gymnastico et palaestrico hoc habemus,: palaestrici motūs,the motions of a dancingmaster,: magister,; cf. doctores,: facies decora et suci palaestrici plena,.—Sarcastically of Verres: palaestricus praetor, because he illegally decided a cause in favor of a company of wrestlers,.—
